content: Certainly. 1. Early child development refers to the progressive acquisition of a child’s abilities to see, hear, move, speak, understand, think, and solve problems. It also encompasses physical growth and nutritional status. If there are other aspects you associate with this term, please specify. 2. Do you have any programs in place that support early child development? If no, proceed to question 16. If not mentioned, do you have a program specifically for Care for Child Development? Response options: 1 = Yes; 2 = No. 3. Is this training currently being implemented or planned? How many health workers in your clinic have received or will receive this training? Please include pediatricians, family doctors, nurses, and other health workers. If possible, provide the total number of potential trainees. 4. Do you have any community outreach programs for early child development? Response options: 1 = Yes; 2 = No. If yes, please specify the details of these programs. Have the community outreach workers been trained? If so, how were they trained? 5. Are there materials or job aids available for health workers or community workers on early child development? If yes, what types of materials are available? Who is responsible for monitoring and implementing these materials? Is this information integrated into a government database? Response options: 1 = Yes; 2 = No. 6. How important do you think early child development is for a child’s health? Response options: 1 = Very important. 2 = Important. 3 = Somewhat important. 4 = Not very important. What do you think needs to be done to improve early child development? 7. How many children aged 0–3 years do you see daily in your clinic? On average, how much time do you spend with each child and their family? During how many sessions per day do you discuss child development with families? How many children aged 0–3 years receive Care for Child Development recommendations from the chart daily? 8. Have you received training on Care for Child Development? If no, proceed to the competencies section. If yes, who provided the training? When did the training occur, and how long did it last (in days)? Did the training include opportunities to practice the recommendations with children? 9. Do you have any other training on early child development? Response options: 1 = Yes; 2 = No. Do you have materials on parenting or child development for families? Response options: 1 = Yes; 2 = No. What would help you perform your job better in terms of caring for child development? 10. Are the following items available in your clinic? At least two toys for infants and young children. Books for young children. Posters or charts on child development (excluding massage-related materials). Videos on child development. Handouts for parents on child development. 11. Regarding your competencies, please assess the following: Do you have adequate knowledge about the physical growth of young children? Do you have adequate knowledge about the cognitive and social development of young children? Do you have adequate knowledge about children’s nutrition? Can you effectively use listening and understanding techniques when communicating with families? Are you able to recognize and praise what parents are doing correctly during sessions? Do you have the skills to counsel fathers and other family members? Can you communicate effectively with young children and infants? Are you able to counsel families on age-appropriate play activities for young children? Can you counsel families on ways to communicate with young children that are appropriate for their age? Are you able to assist families concerned about slow cognitive or physical development in their children? Can you identify problems and counsel families about maternal depression? Do you have the skills to assess the development of young children during sessions? Are you able to provide case management for children with developmental difficulties? Can you guide families of young children with special healthcare needs? 12. For families, do you engage in the following activities with children aged 0–3 years? Reading books or looking at picture books. Telling stories. Singing songs. Taking the child outside the home or compound. Playing with the child. Spending time naming, counting, or drawing things with the child. If yes, who engages in these activities (mother, father, or another family member)? 13. What types of toys or objects does the child play with at home? Items that make music or noise, such as rattles. Drawing or writing materials. Picture books (not schoolbooks). Items for stacking, constructing, or building (e.g., blocks). Items for movement (e.g., balls, bats). Toys for learning shapes and colors. Pretend play items (e.g., dolls, tea sets). Bright and colorful objects for visual stimulation. Have you or anyone in your family made toys for the child? Does the child play with household objects? How often do you play with your child to help them learn new things? Response options: 1 = Not at all. 2 = A few days a week but not every day. 3 = Once or twice every day. 4 = More than twice daily.
